summary: Describes LDAP schema for representing X.509 certificates, X.521 security information and related elements in directories. These replace the definitions in RFC 2252 and RFC 2256. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This document tells directory servers how to store and search X.509 certificates. It defines the attributes that hold certificates and revocation lists, the rules for comparing them, and the classes that say which entries may carry them. It replaces the older schema in RFC 2252 and RFC 2256.

subtitle: How LDAP directories store and search X.509 certificates, revocation lists and related security data.

tldr.problem: Directories reached through LDAP had no single up-to-date way to hold X.509 certificates, revocation lists and related security information.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines LDAP syntaxes, matching rules, attribute types and object classes for a subset of X.509 and X.521, with certificate values encoded in DER and transferred only with the binary option.
tldr.outcome: It replaces the X.509 schema in RFC 2252 and RFC 2256, obsoletes RFC 2587, adds the pkiUser, pkiCA and deltaCRL classes, and deprecates the older classes in favour of pkiUser and pkiCA.

facts.label: Encoding of stored certificates
facts.value: DER, transferred with the binary option

today: RFC 4523 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2006. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It replaced the X.509 schema parts of RFC 2252 and RFC 2256 and obsoleted RFC 2587.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 4523 provides LDAP schema definitions for a subset of the elements specified in X.509 and X.521. It includes attribute types for certificates, cross certificate pairs and certificate revocation lists, matching rules to be used with these attribute types, and related object classes. LDAP syntax definitions are also provided for the associated assertion and attribute values.

The semantics of these elements are as defined in X.509 and X.521, so knowledge of those two standards is necessary to make use of the schema defined here. The definitions are written in the LDAP description formats of RFC 4512 and are line wrapped for readability.

Together with RFC 4510, this document obsoletes RFC 2252 and RFC 2256 in their entirety. The changes made since those two documents are the addition of the pkiUser, pkiCA and deltaCRL classes; the update of attribute types to include equality matching rules in accordance with their X.500 specifications; the addition of certificate, certificate pair, certificate list and algorithm identifier matching rules; and the addition of LDAP syntax for the assertion syntaxes of those matching rules. This document also obsoletes RFC 2587. The X.509 schema descriptions for LDAPv2 are Historic, as is LDAPv2 itself.
sections.plainLanguage: This document tells directory servers how to store and search X.509 certificates. It defines the attributes that hold certificates and revocation lists, the rules for comparing them, and the classes that say which entries may carry them. It replaces the older schema in RFC 2252 and RFC 2256.

sections.title: Syntaxes
sections.content:
The syntaxes describe how LDAP transfers certificates and related data types. Four of them carry X.509 data whose definition has changed over time, so no LDAP-specific encoding is defined for them. Values of these syntaxes SHOULD be encoded using Distinguished Encoding Rules and MUST only be transferred using the ;binary transfer option of RFC 4522, that is, by requesting and returning values using attribute descriptions such as userCertificate;binary.

  • Certificate (1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.115.121.1.8): a value of this syntax is an X.509 Certificate.
  • CertificateList (1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.115.121.1.9): a value of this syntax is an X.509 CertificateList.
  • CertificatePair (1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.115.121.1.10): a value of this syntax is an X.509 CertificatePair.
  • SupportedAlgorithm (1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.115.121.1.49): a value of this syntax is an X.509 SupportedAlgorithm.

As values of these syntaxes contain digitally signed data, the values and the form of each value MUST be preserved as presented.

Seven further syntaxes cover the values a client sends in a search filter. Values of these syntaxes MUST be encoded using the Generic String Encoding Rules of RFC 3641: CertificateExactAssertion, CertificateAssertion, CertificatePairExactAssertion, CertificatePairAssertion, CertificateListExactAssertion, CertificateListAssertion and AlgorithmIdentifier, with object identifiers 1.3.6.1.1.15.1 through 1.3.6.1.1.15.7. Appendix A of the RFC gives an equivalent ABNF grammar for each of them.
sections.plainLanguage: Directory servers store certificates in their signed byte form. The document defines four syntaxes for stored values and seven more for the values a client types into a search. Stored certificates use the binary transfer option, so they cannot be altered in transit. Search values are written as text instead.

sections.title: Matching Rules
sections.content:
The matching rules are the comparisons a directory performs when a client searches. They are intended to act in accordance with their X.500 counterparts. Each rule names the syntax of the value it accepts and the clause of X.509 that defines the comparison.

  • certificateExactMatch (2.5.13.34) compares the presented certificate exact assertion value with an attribute value of the certificate syntax.
  • certificateMatch (2.5.13.35) compares the presented certificate assertion value with an attribute value of the certificate syntax.
  • certificatePairExactMatch (2.5.13.36) and certificatePairMatch (2.5.13.37) do the same for certificate pairs.
  • certificateListExactMatch (2.5.13.38) and certificateListMatch (2.5.13.39) do the same for certificate lists.
  • algorithmIdentifierMatch (2.5.13.40) compares a presented algorithm identifier with an attribute value of the supported algorithm syntax.

The pattern is the same for the three certificate kinds. There is an exact rule that demands a full match, and a second rule that takes an assertion instead. The assertion grammar in Appendix A shows that this second form can carry selected fields of a certificate, such as the serial number, the issuer or the validity dates, and leave the rest out.
sections.plainLanguage: These rules say how a directory compares what a client asked for with what it has stored. Each certificate kind gets an exact rule, which demands a complete match, and a second rule, which can match on selected fields such as the serial number or the issuer.

sections.title: Attribute Types
sections.content:
The attribute types say which LDAP attribute holds each kind of X.509 data, and each one names the matching rule used for equality tests.

  • userCertificate (2.5.4.36) holds the X.509 certificates issued to the user by one or more certificate authorities.
  • cACertificate (2.5.4.37) holds the X.509 certificates issued to the certificate authority.
  • crossCertificatePair (2.5.4.40) holds an X.509 certificate pair.
  • certificateRevocationList (2.5.4.39) and authorityRevocationList (2.5.4.38) hold certificate lists.
  • deltaRevocationList (2.5.4.53) holds certificate lists.
  • supportedAlgorithms (2.5.4.52) holds supported algorithms.

As required by the syntax of each attribute type, the values of these attributes MUST be requested and transferred using the attribute description with the ;binary option, such as userCertificate;binary and certificateRevocationList;binary.
sections.plainLanguage: Seven attribute types say what is stored where. One holds the certificates issued to a user, one holds the certificates issued to an authority, one holds an X.509 certificate pair, three hold revocation lists, and one holds the algorithms the entry supports. Each is always transferred in binary form.

sections.title: Object Classes
sections.content:
The object classes say which entries may carry the certificate data. Some of them add an attribute to an entry that already exists, and one of them defines an entry of its own.

  • pkiUser (2.5.6.21) is used to augment entries for objects that may be subject to certificates, and MAY hold a userCertificate.
  • pkiCA (2.5.6.22) is used to augment entries for objects that act as certificate authorities, and MAY hold cACertificate, certificateRevocationList, authorityRevocationList and crossCertificatePair.
  • cRLDistributionPoint (2.5.6.19) represents objects that act as CRL distribution points. It is structural, MUST have a cn, and MAY hold certificateRevocationList, authorityRevocationList and deltaRevocationList.
  • deltaCRL (2.5.6.23) augments entries to hold delta revocation lists.
  • userSecurityInformation (2.5.6.18) augments entries with the additional associated security information of X.521 clause 6.16, and MAY hold supportedAlgorithms.

Three older classes remain but are deprecated. strongAuthenticationUser (2.5.6.15) is deprecated in favour of pkiUser. certificationAuthority (2.5.6.16) and certificationAuthority-V2 (2.5.6.16.2) are deprecated in favour of pkiCA.
sections.plainLanguage: The object classes say which entries may carry certificates. pkiUser adds certificates to a person or device. pkiCA adds them to an authority. cRLDistributionPoint defines a standalone entry for serving revocation lists. Two older classes are still allowed but marked as deprecated, and new deployments should use pkiUser and pkiCA instead.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
General certificate considerations apply to LDAP-aware certificate applications, and the general LDAP security considerations apply as well.

While elements of certificate information are commonly signed, these signatures only protect the integrity of the signed information. In the absence of data integrity protections in LDAP, or in a lower layer such as IPsec, a server is not assured that a client certificate request, or other request, was unaltered in transit. Likewise, a client cannot be assured that the results of the query were unaltered in transit. Hence it is generally recommended that implementations make use of the authentication and data integrity services in LDAP, described in RFC 4513 and RFC 4511.
sections.plainLanguage: Certificates are signed, but that only protects the certificate itself. Without protection at the LDAP layer or below, a request or a result can be changed on the way. The RFC therefore recommends using the authentication and integrity services LDAP offers.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The IANA has registered an LDAP Object Identifier for use in this specification, and has updated the LDAP Descriptor registry with the names, object identifiers and usages listed in the document. The registrations cover the seven matching rules, the seven attribute types and the eight object classes, and several of them are marked as updates to previous registrations.
sections.plainLanguage: The document asks IANA to register the new names and object identifiers it introduces, and to update the ones that already existed. That keeps every directory implementation using the same identifiers.

items.desc: Augments entries that act as certificate authorities. MAY hold CA certificates and revocation lists.
